newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK grapples with scandal of ousted immigration boss.
newsitem.headline: HK grapples with scandal of ousted immigration boss.

text.p: Hong Kong grappled with a ballooning scandal on Wednesday as the government said it ousted its immigration chief last July after corruption investigators found he had undisclosed business links.

Personnel chief Lam Woon-kwong's testimony to an inquiry panel of Hong Kong's Legislative Council (Legco) cast new light on the case, but lawmakers were skeptical and believed there might be more to come.
Chief Secretary Anson Chan, Hong Kong's second-ranking official, was called to testify next week, and her boss, Governor Chris Patten, may be asked to follow suit later.

Lam, Secretary of the Civil Service, was quizzed by the panel for four hours, disclosing the government had lost confidence in former Immigration Director Laurence Leung's personal integrity before he suddenly stepped down last July.

Leung, 55, spent seven years as head of immigration and 31 years in the Civil Service, and held a highly sensitive post, with strong security implications in the period running up to China's takeover of the British colony on July 1 this year.
He was responsible for areas such as issuing of passports and visas, immigration and border controls, and was privy to sensitive information in handover talks with China.
Lam's unprecedented statement came after six months of intense pressure and conspiracy theories from politicians and the media, and allegations of a cover-up.
It also marked an about-turn in the government's public stance on the case. Both Leung and the government initially said he retired for "personal reasons".

Leung, who had said his personal reasons included grief over his daughter's murder in a cross-bow attack in Canada three years ago, also did a U-turn when he testified at the inquiry last week, saying he had been forced to quit.
Lam dismissed speculation carried by the media in Britain and elsewhere that Leung had been ousted for spying for China.
"It has to do with his character. But I have never had information to allegations of him leaking confidential information," Lam told the inquiry panel.
"As far as I know, we have no evidence that Laurence Leung has done this... as far as we know these allegations are baseless," Lam said.
A sign the scandal may snowball came with the panel's decision to summon Chan to testify on January 23. She is the most senior official to be called in so far.
Patten is also likely to be summoned at some stage, said legislator Ip Kwok-him, who chairs the inquiry.

Lam told the panel that an anti-corruption investigation showed Leung had undisclosed shareholdings, had a business relationship with a legislator, had invested in a Chinese enterprise and had failed to repay a government housing loan.
He said Leung used the HK$1.76 million (US$228,000) housing loan to buy property in Canada which he subsequently sold.

But while the probe by the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) failed to prove suspicions of criminal offences, Lam said Leung had failed a regular conduct assessment and that the graft probe raised questions about his integrity.
"The ICAC investigation has uncovered information which causes us to have great doubt on Mr Leung's suitability to remain in the service," Lam said.
"The conclusion is that he could not pass the integrity test. He failed the test," he told the inquiry panel.

Legislators were unimpressed with the reasons the government said were behind its loss of faith in Leung, who was given less than a day to retire voluntarily or be forced by the government to do so through a disciplinary regulation.

"You have to scrape the end of the barrel to come up with these reasons," Liberal Party legislator and panelist Ronald Arculli told Lam. "Do you really think the public and this committee would be convinced that the government did this for these reasons?"
Leung, the man at the centre of the scandal, said he was relieved after Lam's statement.
"I want to thank the government for clarifying that the (spy) accusation by the British press is groundless. At least I'm clear on this matter," he told reporters outside his home.
